title: Why records misrepresented bands: Mildred and Basie
summary: A 1944 radio program is the only recording where Mildred sounds like herself; Basie records also failed.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I'm glad I have it, it's a 1944 radio program with Mildred and Red on it and it's one of the only times I've heard Mildred recording where she sounds like Mildred.
She didn't record the way she really sang?
Did you ever hear a Basie record of that period that sounded like Basie? Not really; they always did something somewhere.
It's hard for me to tell, because the only time I've heard Basie live is in the sixties and seventies
when his style was altogether different.

Well it was a roaring band. I heard them first in the Grand Terrace in Chicago and it always had that same thing, but never on a record. It had to do with putting limiters on the top and bottom, I guess.
Well with the dynamic range, sure.
The rhythm section was never placed right, it was either off or it was too close, or one thing or another. It never sounded right.
Well, Mildred had that thing too. She was never as loose on a record as she was on this '44 record.
I remember in rooms how she would sound and in Novello's band, it was never recorded either. It had a much different thing about it than records showed.
It was like before when I spoke about walking into a room and hearing a band.
